clinicalPearls: Obstruction to right ventricular outflow at valve level, usually congenital and often due to a domed, fused pliable valve, though dysplastic valves occur in Noonan syndrome

Signs include an ejection systolic click that decreases with inspiration, an ejection systolic murmur loudest at the left upper sternal edge (pulmonary area), and a widely split second heart sound with a soft pulmonary component as severity increases
Mild stenosis is common, frequently asymptomatic, and tends not to progress, whereas moderate to severe obstruction produces exertional breathlessness, fatigue, and eventually right heart failure
The right ventricle hypertrophies to overcome the gradient, and severe long-standing obstruction can cause tricuspid regurgitation and raised right atrial pressure
Balloon valvuloplasty is the treatment of choice for a suitable pliable domed valve and gives durable relief in most patients
Dysplastic and heavily calcified valves respond poorly to balloon dilatation and may need surgical valvotomy or valve replacement
Echocardiography with Doppler estimation of the peak gradient guides the timing of intervention alongside symptoms and right ventricular changes
reference.pathophysiology: In valvular pulmonary stenosis the pulmonary valve is narrowed, most often by commissural fusion of a congenitally domed valve or by thickened, poorly mobile dysplastic leaflets. The obstruction imposes a pressure load on the right ventricle, which hypertrophies to maintain output across the narrowed orifice; the resulting high-velocity jet produces post-stenotic dilatation of the pulmonary trunk. With severe, chronic obstruction the hypertrophied right ventricle may fail, right atrial pressure rises, and any coexisting atrial communication can permit right-to-left shunting with cyanosis. Relief of the gradient allows the ventricular hypertrophy to regress over time.
additionalDifferentials: Supravalvular pulmonary or branch pulmonary artery stenosis
Atrial septal defect with a pulmonary flow murmur
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler to localise the obstruction and estimate the peak gradient
Assessment of right ventricular size, hypertrophy, and function and of tricuspid regurgitation
Cardiac MRI to quantify right ventricular volumes and clarify the level of obstruction
Electrocardiography and chest radiography for right ventricular hypertrophy and post-stenotic pulmonary artery dilatation
Right heart catheterisation when non-invasive gradient assessment is discordant or before balloon valvuloplasty
redFlags: Exertional syncope or presyncope indicating severe obstruction
Signs of right heart failure with raised jugular venous pressure and peripheral oedema
Cyanosis from right-to-left shunting through an atrial communication
Severe stenosis with a dysplastic or calcified valve unsuitable for balloon treatment
reference.prognosis: Mild pulmonary stenosis carries an excellent outlook and rarely progresses, while moderate to severe obstruction responds well to balloon valvuloplasty or surgery with durable relief and regression of right ventricular hypertrophy.
pitfalls: Overlooking a dysplastic valve, especially in Noonan syndrome, that will respond poorly to balloon valvuloplasty
Attributing the murmur to an innocent flow murmur and missing significant obstruction
Failing to recognise coexisting infundibular obstruction that persists after valve relief
Not assessing for an atrial communication that may allow cyanosis in severe disease
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
